comments.text:
PlotCharAndColour - the games ONE drawing primitive, called from 35 sites.
In:  plotColumn ($02) = X 0-39, plotRow ($03) = Y 0-23,
     plotChar ($04) = screen code, plotColour ($05) = colour nibble.
Writes plotChar to $0400+row*40+col, then adds $D4 to the pointer high
byte ($04 -> $D8) and writes plotColour to the matching colour-RAM cell.
This is why a search for stores into $D800-$DBE7 finds almost nothing:
every coloured character in Gridrunner goes through here, indirectly.
$8180-$8185 (LDA $07 / LDA $07 / STA $07) is dead: it loads and stores
the same value twice and changes nothing. Timing padding or leftovers.

Set screenPtr ($06/$07) to the start of row plotRow ($03), and leave
Y = plotColumn ($02) so the caller can use ($06),Y. The row bases come
from the split table screenRowLo/$0340 and screenRowHi/$0360 built by
InitVicSidClearScreen - a multiply-free row lookup, the standard C64 idiom.

ReadScreenChar - the inverse of PlotCharAndColour: returns the screen
code currently at (plotColumn, plotRow) in A. Gridrunner does collision
detection by reading the screen back, so the picture IS the game state:
there is no separate sprite list to test against.

Video and sound bring-up, plus screen clear.
$02/$03 are pointed at $D000 and the VIC registers are written through
STA ($02),Y with the register offset in Y - which is why a plain search
for stores into $D000-$D02E finds only three of them:
  Y=$18 -> $D018 = $18  screen at $0400, character base at $2000
  Y=$20 -> $D020 = $00  border black
  Y=$21 -> $D021 = $00  background black
SID: V1FREQHI=$0A, V1AD=$0A, V2AD=$0A ($0 attack, $A decay),
V1SR=V2SR=$00 (no sustain - percussive), V2FREQHI=$05.
Then it builds the 24-entry screen row address table at $0340/$0360 and
fills all 24x40 cells with $20 (the blank glyph in this font).

Retrigger voices 1 and 2: CTRL=$00 (gate off) then CTRL=$81.
$81 = %10000001 = noise waveform + gate on. Both voices are noise, which
is the whole of Gridrunners explosion/zap palette - there is no music.

Copy the 512-byte character set from characterSetData ($8E00-$8FFF) to
$2000-$21FF, where $D018 = $18 tells the VIC to look for it.
X counts 0,255,254..1 (DEX before BNE) so all 256 bytes of each page are
moved. Only 64 characters exist - screen codes $00-$3F - so the game uses
no glyph above $3F.

The complete character set: 64 glyphs, 8 bytes each, copied to $2000.
It is a CUSTOM font, so no built-in PETSCII or screen-code table reads it.
The mapping, read off the glyph bitmaps:
  $00 grid intersection (+)   $01-$1A game objects: ships, droids,
  explosion frames, the pod/diamond, laser dots, starfield specks
  $1B $1C Y      $1D H(small)  $1E R(small)  $1F up-arrow
  $20 space
  $21 G  $22 R  $23 U  $24 I  $25 D  $26 N  $27 E  $28 A  $29 B
  $2A F  $2B H  $2C J  $2D M  $2E P  $2F S
  $30 O and 0 (one glyph serves both)
  $31-$39 digits 1-9
  $3A T  $3B V  $3C $3D the two halves of a (c) symbol  $3E L  $3F |
Letters absent from the font: C K Q W X Z. The alphabet is packed in the
order Minter needed it, not A-Z, which is why every built-in encoding
renders the games text as nonsense. Verified by decoding $8080 to
"(c) 1982 HES  PRESS FIRE TO BEGIN" and $8DE1 to "BY JEFF MINTER".

args.text:
Structure is in. Key facts, in case they save you time:

* $8000-$8008 is a CBM80 autostart header, NOT code. Real entry is $83C1 (ColdStart); $83E2 is the NMI stub.
* $8E00-$8FFF is a 64-char charset, copied to $2000-$21FF at $82EC before anything else. $D018=$18 (screen $0400, charset $2000).
* I decoded the charset by hand. The mapping is NOT ASCII and NOT screen codes:
  $20 space, $30-$39 = digits 0-9 ($30 doubles as the letter O),
  $21=G $22=R $23=U $24=I $25=D $26=N $27=E $28=A $29=B $2A=F $2B=H $2C=J $2D=M $2E=P $2F=S $3A=T $3B=V $3E=L $1B=Y,
  $3C/$3D = the two halves of a (c) symbol, $3F = vertical grid bar.
  So $8080 reads "(c) 1982 HES  PRESS FIRE TO BEGIN", $8DE1 "BY JEFF MINTER", $8DF1 "ENTER LEVEL 00", $8C51 " BATTLE STATIONS", $8C63 " ENTER GRID AREA 00".
  Declaring these text/petscii/ascii gives nonsense - I am going to add a project decoder for the real mapping.
* Everything the game draws goes through PlotCharAndColour $8172 (35 refs): plotCol $02, plotRow $03, plotChar $04, plotColour $05. ReadCharAtPlotPos $818B is the read side. The game has no sprites at all - collision is done by reading the character already on screen.
* Char meanings so far: $00 empty grid cell, $07 the player ship, $0A a droid bomb, $01/$02 the two zapper glyphs, $0D-$13 and $18 the droid animation frames, $3F the grid bar, $14/$15 something the laser can also hit (scores 3).

I am doing control flow and routine naming; the charset bitmap and the data tables are yours if you want them.

comments.text:
Draw the title-screen copyright line. X counts $20 down to 1 over
LDA $807F,X, so the 32 bytes $8080-$809F land at screen $0593-$05B2 =
row 10, columns 3-34, all in colour $07 (yellow).
Through the games own character set the text reads:
  "(c) 1982 HES  PRESS FIRE TO BEGIN"
($3C and $3D are the left and right halves of the (c) symbol.)

Title-screen copyright string, 32 bytes, in the games custom character
set - NOT PETSCII and NOT C64 screen codes. Reads:
  "(c) 1982 HES  PRESS FIRE TO BEGIN"
Indexed 1-based from $807F, so $8080 is byte 1.

Draw the two centred title-screen lines and set level = 1.
X counts $0E down to 1 over two 1-based strings:
  $8DE0,X -> screen $04FA,X  = row 6, cols 11-24, colour $03 (cyan)
            "BY JEFF MINTER"
  $8DF0,X -> screen $054A,X  = row 8, cols 11-24, colour $01 (white)
            "ENTER LEVEL 00"
The $EA at $8DE0 and $8DF0 is the unused index-0 slot, not text.

Two 14-byte title strings in the games custom character set:
  $8DE1 "BY JEFF MINTER"
  $8DF1 "ENTER LEVEL 00"
Each is indexed 1-based from the $EA byte before it. $8DFF (a space) is
never read. Decode with the projects "Gridrunner custom font text"
decoder; every built-in encoding renders these as nonsense.

Draw the two-digit level number on the title screen. level ($35) wraps
back to 1 at $20, so the selectable range is 1-31. The digits are counted
up rather than divided: increment the units cell, and when it passes $39
(9) reset it to $30 (0) and carry into the tens cell. They are written
straight into screen RAM at $0557/$0558 = row 8, columns 23 and 24, which
is exactly where "ENTER LEVEL 00" left its two 0s.

Title-screen input loop, polling $DC11 - a mirror of $DC01, CIA 1 port B,
which is joystick port 2 wired active-low.
  $EF = bit 4 clear = FIRE     -> $8DC6, start the game
  $FE = bit 0 clear = UP       -> increment level and redraw
Nothing else is tested, so the level chooser is up-only and wraps at 31.

args.text:
beryl: agreed on the split, thanks. Two notes.

1. We independently wrote the same charset decoder within a minute (yours dec_3g1jgm, mine dec_wd8txj) with the same mapping - I have removed mine, yours stands. That is two of us paying the same cost because the tool that would have prevented it (list_decoders before writing one) is not something either of us thought to call on a project we knew was empty. Worth noting for the log.

2. Correction to your $30: it is both. The score code at $8870 increments $040F..$0415 and wraps at $3A, so $30-$39 really are digits 0-9; but $8080 spells "TO" as $3A $30 and $8C63 spells "STATIONS" with $30 for the O. One glyph, two readings, decided by context - which is exactly the case re64 models with add_label/bind_label for addresses and has no equivalent of for character codes.

3. There are no sprites. $D015 is never written; the only $D000-page writes are $D018 and $D020/$D021, and those go through a ZP pointer ($02/$03 = $D000, STA ($02),Y with Y=$18/$20/$21) at InitVicSidAndScreen $8100 - so a plain range search on $D000-$D02E will find nothing. Everything visible is characters plotted through $8172.

Big one for whoever is reading text: the game ships its OWN character set at $8E00-$8FFF (64 glyphs), copied to $2000 by $82EC, with $D018=$18 set at $8100. The alphabet is NOT in A-Z order, so PETSCII and screen-code both render the games strings as garbage. Mapping: $20 space; $21-$2F = G R U I D N E A B F H J M P S; $30 = O and 0 sharing one glyph; $31-$39 = 1-9; $3A T, $3B V, $3E L, $3C/$3D = the two halves of (c), $3F = |, $1B/$1C = Y, $1F = up-arrow. C K Q W X Z do not exist in the font. I stored a decoder (dec_3g1jgm, "Gridrunner custom font text") and pointed the two text regions at it, so $8080 now renders as "(c) 1982 HES  PRESS FIRE TO BEGIN" and $8DE1 as "BY JEFF MINTER" / "ENTER LEVEL 00" right in the listing. If you find more text anywhere, set_region kind=text view=snippet:dec_3g1jgm and it will read.

Also: $8172 (35 callers) is the ONE plot primitive - char in $04, colour in $05, col in $02, row in $03; it writes screen then adds $D4 to the pointer high byte to hit colour RAM. $818B reads a screen cell back, which is how collision detection works: the picture is the game state.

args.name: droidAnimFrameTable
args.comment: Droid animation/damage frames, indexed 1..7: $18,$0D,$0E,$0F,$10,$11,$12. AnimateDroidsOnScreen $86D7 walks the whole playfield and advances any character found here to the next frame; LaserHitsChar $87CB walks it backwards, so a laser hit knocks a droid back one frame instead of killing it.

Reads "GRIDRUNNER" then a 2-char SC icon, 7 score digits, a 2-char HI icon, 7 hi-score digits, the ship glyph $07, and the lives digit. Note the copy loop runs X=$28..1 over table-1, so the LAST byte it fetches is $8847 - the first byte of statusLineColourTable, $34 = the character 4. The initial 4 lives is literally the first colour byte read one past the end of this table.

args.comment: " ENTER GRID AREA 00", written to $054D-$055F. The trailing 00 at $055E/$055F is then incremented once per level by the loop at $8C9D, so it shows the level number.

args.name: levelParameterTables
args.comment: Three parallel 32-entry tables indexed by level ($35), read at $8C8C. $8CB4 -> wavesLeft ($2A), $8CD4 -> droidsPerWave ($2B), $8CF4 -> zapperFireInterval ($34). Waves rise 1,2,2,3.. to 7; droids per wave rise to $18; the zapper interval falls from $19 to $05, so later levels fire the beams more often. Level select on the title screen is capped at $20, and these tables are exactly $20 entries - so every reachable level has parameters.

args.name: textEnterLevel

args.name: textEnterGridArea

The trailing 00 at $055E/$055F is then incremented once per level by the loop at $8C9D, so it reads as the level number. 18 bytes, not 19: $8C75 is the next instruction and my first attempt at this region swallowed it, which cost 26 instructions of decode.

comments.text: COLD START. The KERNAL reset routine jumps here through the $8000 cartridge vector, before it has finished its own initialisation, so this routine has to do the rest by hand: IOINIT ($FDA3), RAMTAS ($FD50), RESTOR ($FD15) and CINT ($E518). SCROLX=$05 first, which is 38-column mode with a horizontal scroll of 5. LDA #$08 / JSR CHROUT sends the control code that LOCKS the character set, so nothing can flip to lower case and destroy the game's own font. Then straight into CopyCharsetToRam; it never returns and there is no RTS.

The $8002 half of the cartridge vector, which the KERNAL uses as the NMI entry - i.e. RESTORE. It pulls the three registers the NMI handler pushed and RTIs, so pressing RESTORE does nothing at all. That is the point: it makes the game unbreakable from the keyboard. It is also why the block analysis reports this routine with a stack delta of -3 rather than the ordinary -2.

Copy the 512-byte font from $8E00-$8FFF to $2000-$21FF, where $D018 will point the VIC at it. Two 256-byte copies in one loop with X starting at 0, so the first iteration handles offset 0 and the loop runs the full 256 - the standard DEX/BNE-from-zero idiom. Nothing in the game ever reads $8E00 again.

One-time hardware and screen init, entered from CopyCharsetToRam and never called.

It writes the VIC through a zero-page pointer rather than absolutely: $02/$03 are set to $D000 and then STA ($02),Y with Y=$18, $20, $21 writes $D018 (screen $0400, charset $2000) and clears the border and background to black. A range search over $D000-$D02E finds none of these three writes - they are the only VIC register writes in the whole program, and there are no sprites at all.

Then the SID envelopes, then the row-address table: for each of 24 rows it stores the low byte of the row base in screenRowLo and the high byte in screenRowHi and fills the row with $20. That table is what makes PlotCharAndColour a handful of instructions instead of a multiply.
Turn (plotCol, plotRow) into a screen pointer: screenPtr = screenRowLo/Hi[plotRow], Y = plotCol. The whole game addresses the screen this way.

PLOT. Writes plotChar to the screen and plotColour to colour RAM at (plotCol, plotRow). 35 callers - every single thing this game draws goes through here, because there are no sprites.

The colour address is derived by adding $D4 to the high byte of the screen pointer: $04xx + $D400 = $D8xx. That works only because the screen is at $0400 and colour RAM at $D800, and it is why moving the screen would break the game.

$8180-$8185 is three dead instructions - LDA $07 / LDA $07 / STA $07 - six wasted bytes that load a value and store it back to where it came from. Almost certainly the remains of an edit.

Read the character currently at (plotCol, plotRow). This is the game's entire collision system: instead of comparing coordinates, it asks the screen what is already in the cell it is about to move into. Nine callers, and every one of them is a collision test.

Read joystick port 1 and invert it into `joystick`. The address is $DC11, which is not a documented register - CIA1's sixteen registers repeat every 16 bytes through $DC00-$DCFF, so $DC11 is $DC01, port B. EOR #$FF turns the active-low switches into active-high bits: bit0 up, bit1 down, bit2 left, bit3 right, bit4 fire.

THE MAIN LOOP. Three addresses form one cycle: MainLoopTop $83A0 jumps here, here calls the player and the pause check and jumps to MainLoopUpdates $83A3, which calls nine update routines and jumps to MainLoopDelay $83E8, which burns 21 iterations of DEX and jumps back to MainLoopTop.

There is no interrupt and no raster sync anywhere in the program - the NMI vector is a bare RTI and no IRQ vector is ever installed. The loop free-runs, so the game's speed is whatever this code takes, and every subsystem is paced by counting iterations rather than frames.

Two counters do that pacing and they are read at different values by different subsystems, which is how the work is spread out:
  tick $0D - decremented by UpdatePlayer, never reloaded, so it free-runs mod 256. UpdatePlayer acts at 0, UpdateZappers at 1, ExplosionSfxStep on odd values, ReloadTickIfWrapped forces it to $80 at $FF.
  phase $0F - decremented by UpdateLaser, reloaded to $18. UpdateLaser acts at 0, FireZapperBeam at 5.
So `CMP #$05 / BEQ` at the top of a routine is not a magic number, it is a time slot.

The nine per-iteration updates, in order: laser, zappers, zapper beam, droid animation, bombs, explosion sound, droids, tick reload, wave-cleared check. Each one begins by testing its own counter and returning immediately if this is not its slot, so most iterations run almost nothing.

The whole of the game's frame pacing: 21 iterations of DEX/BNE. That is roughly 100 microseconds, so it does not pace anything by itself - it exists to stop the loop being quite as tight as it otherwise would be. Note $83F0-$83FF is unreachable NOP filler with a stray JMP MainLoopTop at $83FA that nothing jumps to.

UPDATE PLAYER, and the sole reader of the joystick. Runs when tick reaches 0, i.e. every 256 iterations of the main loop.

Order matters and is worth reading carefully:
1. Look at the cell the player is standing in. If it does not still hold the ship glyph $07, something has been drawn over the player since last time - DieUnlessHarmlessChar decides whether that is fatal.
2. Erase the old position to the empty grid cell (char $00, colour 8).
3. Apply the joystick to plotCol/plotRow, each direction clamped: columns 1..$26, rows $0F..$15. The row range is six rows deep at the bottom of the grid, which is the band the player is confined to.
4. Look at the cell being moved INTO. If it is not empty, PlayerRanIntoChar.
5. Save the new position to playerCol/playerRow and draw the ship, char $07 colour $0D.

The clamping is written as `if it went one past, put it back`, not as a comparison before moving, so the player briefly occupies an illegal coordinate inside this routine.

UPDATE LASER - the player's shot. One shot at a time: laserRow = $FF means no shot in flight, and fire is only read when it is $FF.

A shot is launched from the player's cell one row up, with laserChar $08 and a sound counter of $40. On each step it looks at the cell ahead; anything that is not empty and not the laser's own glyph goes to LaserHitsChar. laserChar counts $08 -> $0A and then the shot advances one row up and resets to $08, so the glyph animates as it travels. Reaching row 2 (the top of the grid) retires the shot.

There is exactly one laser slot in the whole program, which is why the fire button does nothing while a shot is on screen.

UPDATE ZAPPERS - the two edge sweepers. One walks down column 0 (leftZapperRow, rows 3..$15, glyph $01), the other walks along row $16 (bottomZapperCol, columns 1..$26, glyph $02). Each step erases with $20 and redraws.

When zapperFireCountdown runs out it is reloaded from zapperFireInterval - a per-level value - and a beam is armed: beamActive=$FF, and the two zappers' current positions are frozen into beamRow/beamVertCol for FireZapperBeam to use. That is the mechanic: the beams fire from wherever the sweepers happen to be, so the danger is predictable if you watch them.

FIRE ZAPPER BEAM. Runs when phase is 5 and beamActive is $FF.

Draws the vertical beam down column beamVertCol from row $15 to row 2, then advances the horizontal beam one column along row beamRow. CharIsPlayerThenDie $8020 is what checks the cell the horizontal beam is entering, so the beam kills by walking into the player rather than by any coordinate comparison. When the beam reaches its own leading character the sweep is over and $86A2 erases the vertical line and clears beamActive.

ANIMATE DROIDS - and it is a screen scan, not an object loop. Every $05 of zapperFireCountdown it walks the whole playfield, $0450 to $07FF, one byte at a time through scanPtr, and for any character it finds in droidAnimFrameTable it writes the next frame back. A droid on the last frame calls DroidDropsBomb.

This is why the animation state of a droid is not in any array: it IS the character code on the screen. Damage works the same way - LaserHitsChar walks the same table backwards. The screen is the model.

A droid at the end of its animation drops a bomb. It writes glyph $0A at the droid's own cell and then looks for a free slot in bombPtrHi (scanning down from 24 for the $FF marker) and stores the current scanPtr there. If every slot is busy it writes glyph $12 instead and the bomb simply does not exist - a silent cap of 24 bombs in flight.

UPDATE BOMBS, every $40 iterations. Walks the 24 slots and steps each live one. The slots hold a raw screen pointer split across bombPtrLo/bombPtrHi rather than a column and a row, so moving down a row is just adding 40 - see MoveOneBomb.

Move one bomb down one row. Reads the cell it is in (if that is the ship glyph $07, the player is dead), erases it, adds $28 to the pointer, then reads the destination: $20 means it has fallen off the bottom of the playfield and the slot is freed with $FF; $07 is again death; anything else and it draws itself in white.

Note it does NOT go through PlotCharAndColour: it computes the colour address itself by adding $D4 to the pointer's high byte, the same trick, because it already holds a pointer and has no column/row to give the plot routine.

THE LASER HIT THIS CHARACTER. Search droidAnimFrameTable for it. Not found, so it is not a droid: LaserHitOtherChar. Found at index n: step BACK one frame - so a hit damages a droid rather than killing it, and a droid takes as many hits as its frame number. Index 1 is the last one: the cell is erased, ScoreDroidKill adds 10, and the shot is retired.

Both exits do PLA PLA before returning. This routine discards its own return address and returns to its caller's caller, skipping the rest of UpdateLaser - which is how a hit ends the laser's turn without a flag. It is the reason a naive call graph is wrong about UpdateLaser: the code after the JSR at $8535 is not reached through that call.

Add to the score. X is the digit position within scoreDigits (0 = most significant, 6 = least) and Y is how many times to increment it. Digits are the character codes $30-$39 directly in screen memory - there is no binary score anywhere - and a carry is `wrapped to $30 and DEX`. The score is literally the thing on the screen.

UPDATE DROIDS - the swarm. Three parallel arrays indexed 1..droidCount: droidCol, droidRow, droidFlags, addressed as table-1,X throughout. droidFlags bit7 = drawn, bit6 = squad leader, bits 0/1 = direction, EOR #$03 at $8962 flips them.

A droid steps sideways in its current direction; reaching the bottom row ($16) sends it back to row $0E and forces its direction. Anything non-empty in the way goes through BombPosOrDeath, which is where the ship glyph kills the player.

When a droid is destroyed the array is COMPACTED - $8A53 copies every entry above it down one and decrements droidCount - which is why the flag bits are ORed into the neighbour first at $8AA4: the squad-leader bit has to survive the shuffle.

SPAWN. wavesLeft and droidsPerWave come from the level tables. Droids are created at column $0A row $02 - the top of the grid - one at a time as spawnCountdown expires, with flags $41 (leader + direction) for the first of a wave and $00 for the rest, and $80 for the last, which is what tells WaveClearedCheck the wave is complete.

PLAYER DIES. Five callers, from all over the program and all at different call depths - the beam, a bomb, a droid, a collision. LDX #$F6 / TXS throws the whole call stack away rather than unwinding it, which is the only way to get out of, say, MoveOneBomb three frames deep inside UpdateBombs. That is why this is a jump target and not a subroutine, and why block analysis reports an undefined stack delta here.

DEATH EXPLOSION. Eight fragments burst out from the player's last position in the eight compass directions, using fragCol/fragRow and the delta tables at $8BC0. blastFrames counts 15 steps down; blastChar cycles $16-$18 and a fragment is only redrawn where the cell still holds the character it drew last time, so the explosion does not scribble over anything permanent. When it finishes, LoseALife.

LOSE A LIFE. Clears the playfield, decrements the lives digit - which is a character on the screen at $0427, there is no lives variable - and if it has reached '0' goes to CheckHighScore, i.e. game over. Otherwise RestartSameLevel.

Restart the level just lost. It decrements the lives digit and the level number and then falls into NewLevel, which increments both again - so the two DECs exist purely to cancel NewLevel's INCs. Replaying a level neither advances you nor gives you the free life.

NEW LEVEL. Resets the stack (this is reached by jump, not call), clears the playfield, prints "BATTLE STATIONS" and "ENTER GRID AREA nn", awards a life (the digit at $0427, capped at '9'), advances the level (capped at $20), and reads the three level parameters out of levelParameterTables. Then the fanfare, then StartLevel.

START LEVEL. Draws the grid with DrawGridWipe, plays the materialise effect, then sets the per-level state: player at column $14 row $15 (bottom centre), no laser ($11=$FF), zappers at their starting positions, all 24 bomb slots freed, droidCount 0. Ends by jumping into the main loop and never returns.

$834E-$8357 is five dead instructions: LDA $2B / STA $2B / STA $2B / LDA $2A / STA $2A. They read a value and write it back. NewLevel has already loaded both from the level tables, so this looks like the remains of code that used to compute them here.

TITLE SCREEN. Sets the level to 1, prints "BY JEFF MINTER" and "ENTER LEVEL 00" and the copyright line, then loops in TitleWaitForInput.

The level select is genuinely a level select: joystick up increments `level`, fire starts the game there. It is read at $8DB0 by comparing the raw $DC11 byte against $EF (fire) and $FE (up), rather than through ReadJoystick - a second, independent piece of joystick code with the opposite polarity convention.

GAME OVER: compare the seven score digits against the seven hi-score digits most-significant first. The comparison is on character codes, which works because $30-$39 are contiguous and in order. First digit that differs decides it: BMI means the score is lower, so no new record. Equal all the way through also means no record. Then back to the title screen. Nothing is saved anywhere - it is a cartridge, and the hi-score lives only in screen memory at $041B.

The player is standing on something. $08 and $09 are laser glyphs and $00 is an empty cell, so those are survivable; anything else is fatal. Note what this implies: walking into your own shot is harmless, which is not obvious from the drawing code.
Wave cleared: no waves left AND no droids left means the level is over, so jump to NewLevel. This is the only way to advance a level other than the title-screen select.

Look at the cell at (plotCol, plotRow); if it holds the ship glyph $07, the player is dead. Used by the horizontal zapper beam. The routine returns the character it read, so the caller can also use it as a plain read - which FireZapperBeam does at $868D.

Nine bytes of cartridge header. The KERNAL's reset code looks for the five bytes C3 C2 CD 38 30 ("CBM80" with the top bit set on the first three) at $8004 and, finding them, jumps through $8000 instead of finishing its own startup - so this cartridge takes control before BASIC exists. $8000 = $83C1 (cold start), $8002 = $83E2 (NMI). Declaring this as code, which is what the project did before anyone looked at it, disassembles a vector table.

args.name: levelParameterTables
args.comment:
Three 32-entry tables, read at $8C8C with X = level, 1-based: levelWaves $8CB5-$8CD4 -> wavesLeft, levelDroidsPerWave $8CD5-$8CF4 -> droidsPerWave, levelZapperInterval $8CF5-$8D14 -> zapperFireInterval.

They are indexed as table-1,X and the three bases ($8CB4, $8CD4, $8CF4) are the LAST byte of the preceding thing rather than bytes of their own - $8CB4 is the high byte of the JMP $8D70 at $8CB2. Three bytes saved by never storing an entry 0.

Waves climb 1,2,2,3,3,3,4... to 7. Droids per wave climb from 7 to $18, with a dip at level 14 ($03) that is either a difficulty pause or a typo - nothing distinguishes them. The zapper interval falls from $19 to $05 and then flattens, so past about level 20 the beams fire as fast as they ever will and only the droid count still rises. The title-screen level select is capped at $20 and the tables are exactly $20 entries, so every reachable level has parameters and there is no out-of-range read.

args.name: orphanedCharsetCopyTail
args.comment:
NOT dead filler - this is the tail of the charset copy loop, left behind when the CBM80 header was put over the top of it, and the byte offsets prove it.

The loop that survives at $82EE is: A2 00 / BD 00 8E / 9D 00 20 / BD 00 8F / 9D 00 21 / CA / D0 F1 / 4C 00 81. Lay that out from $8000 and the bytes land at: $8000 A2 00, $8002 BD 00 8E, $8005 9D 00 20, $8008 BD 00 8F, $800B 9D 00 21, $800E CA, $800F D0 F1, $8011 4C 00 81. Everything from $8009 onward is exactly that, byte for byte, including the branch displacement $F1 which resolves to $8002 - the loop head that would have been there. The nine-byte cartridge header covers $8000-$8008 and clipped the opcode of the LDA at $8008; nothing else was touched.

So the charset copy originally lived at the very start of the cartridge, was moved to $82EC when the CBM80 vectors needed the first nine bytes, and the last eleven bytes of the old copy were never removed. It is unreachable: nothing branches or jumps into $8009-$8014.

args.name: strayRts8162
args.comment: An RTS nothing reaches, sitting between the end of InitVicSidAndScreen (which jumps away) and ScreenPtrForPlotRow.

args.name: filler83F0
args.comment: Ten NOPs, a JMP MainLoopTop that nothing reaches, and three more NOPs. The JMP is real code with no caller - most likely the main loop once ended here and MainLoopDelay was inserted at $83E8 in front of it.

args.name: strayRts87D8
args.comment: An RTS after the JMP at $87D5. Unreachable: LaserHitOtherChar is entered by jump and both paths through LaserHitsChar leave by PLA/PLA.

args.name: deadDroidHelpers
args.comment: Two complete little routines with no callers: LDX #$01 / INC droidChar / RTS, and LDX savedX / INX / CPX droidCount / RTS. Both are things UpdateDroids does inline. Removed from the call sites and never deleted.

args.name: deadPlotUnlessPlayer
args.comment: JSR ReadCharAtPlotPos / CMP #$07 / BEQ skip / JMP PlotCharAndColour - a plot-unless-the-player-is-there helper with no callers. Compare PlotDroidIfVisible $8995, which does the same job by testing a flag bit instead of by reading the screen.

args.name: deadBombFallOff
args.comment: CMP #$20 / BEQ back / JMP PlayerDies - the off-the-bottom test that MoveOneBomb now does inline at $87AA. No callers.

args.name: orphanedJumpOperand
args.comment: $8DCB/$8DCC are B0 8D - the operand of a JMP $8DB0 whose 4C opcode is gone - followed by nineteen NOPs to the end of the block. The live JMP $8DB0 is at $8DC3, so this is where TitleShowLevel used to end before $8DC6 was inserted.

args.text:
THE WHOLE OF GRIDRUNNERS SOUND, read off all 66 stores into $D400-$D418.

Registers the game NEVER writes: every FREQLO ($D400 $D407 $D40E), every
pulse width ($D402/3 $D409/A $D410/11), and the entire filter section
($D415-$D417). So: no filter, no pulse waveform, and pitch is set with the
HIGH BYTE ONLY - 256 coarse steps of about 61 Hz. Everything you hear is
deliberately crude, and cheap enough to do inline in the game loop with no
interrupt and no player routine. There is no music anywhere in the cartridge.

Voice 1 - NOISE. CTRL only ever $00 (gate off) then $81 (noise + gate).
  AD = $0A (attack 0, decay 10), SR = $00: a percussive click with no
  sustain, retriggered per event. Used for the grid-wipe tick, the player
  laser, and the death blast.
Voice 2 - NOISE ($81) most of the time, TRIANGLE ($11) in SweepDownSfx
  $8450. AD = $0A, SR = $00, same envelope as voice 1.
Voice 3 - SAWTOOTH ($21) for the zapper beam and the explosion sweep, and
  RING-MODULATED SAWTOOTH ($25) for the level-start fanfare. AD = $04
  (faster decay), SR = $00. Voice 3 is the only one that is ever pitched
  rather than noisy, and it idles at V3FREQHI = $04 between effects.

SIGVOL $D418 is used as a fader, not just an on switch:
  $8414 volume = $0F - fxCounter, so the outward explosion fades as it grows
  $842D/$8437/$843F three sweeps at $0F, $08, $02 - a receding triple chirp
  $8B30 volume = blastFrames, so the death explosion fades with its animation
The filter bits of $D418 are always 0, which is consistent with the filter
registers never being touched.

comments.text:
DRAW THE GRID - the level-start wipe, and the reason the game is called
Gridrunner. Two passes over the same playfield, both in ORANGE ($08):
  pass 1 ($81AE) columns 2..$26, each drawn top to bottom as $3F, the
         vertical-bar glyph. This is the wipe you see travelling right.
  pass 2 ($81ED) rows 2..$15, each drawn left to right as $00, the
         cross glyph - which overwrites the bars and leaves the finished
         grid of + marks the whole game is played on.
Every single cell plotted also calls RetriggerNoiseVoices12, so the wipe
is heard as a stream of noise clicks, one per character.
Between columns WipeSfxDelayAndPitch sets V1FREQHI = gridCol and
V2FREQHI = gridCol+1, so the pitch of the clicks RISES with the column:
the sound sweeps across with the picture.

Inter-column delay for the grid wipe, whose whole job is a side effect.
fxCounter is set to 4 and then INCremented until it wraps back to 4 -
251 iterations - and every iteration writes V1FREQHI = gridCol and
V2FREQHI = gridCol+1 at $8240. So the delay and the pitch sweep are the
same loop: the noise gets higher as the wipe moves right.

Level-start burst: char $16 in WHITE spreading outward from the centre
(row $15, column $14) while fxCounter counts $0F down. Voice 2 is
retriggered as noise on every step, and $8414 sets SIGVOL = $0F - fxCounter
so the burst gets LOUDER as it gets bigger. It ends by planting the ship
glyph $07 in LIGHT_GREEN at the player start position, then three
SweepDownSfx chirps at falling volume ($0F, $08, $02).

A falling chirp on voice 2, and the one place in the game that uses a
TONE rather than noise: CTRL = $11 = triangle + gate. V2FREQHI counts
down from $18 to 1, so the pitch falls. Called three times in a row at
decreasing SIGVOL, which is the sound of the player materialising.

The player laser sound. laserSfx counts down and is written to BOTH
V1FREQHI and V2FREQHI, and both voices are retriggered as noise ($81)
every frame - so it is two noise generators at slightly different
settings sweeping down together, which is what gives the shot its
ragged zap rather than a clean tone. Silent when laserSfx is 0.

Arm the zapper-beam sound: V3FREQHI = $03, about as low as the coarse
high-byte-only pitch control goes. The caller then sets V3CTRL = $21,
sawtooth + gate, so the beam is a low buzzing saw - the only sustained
pitched sound in the game.

The explosion sweep, on voice 3, one step every other tick.
sfxFreq starts at $F0 and is DECremented into V3FREQHI while its top two
bits are still set - i.e. down to $3F - with V3CTRL retriggered to $21
(sawtooth) each step. That is a falling saw. When it bottoms out,
sfxRepeats decides whether to reload $F0 and sweep again, so a bigger kill
sounds like several descending swoops. With nothing left to do it parks
V3FREQHI at $04 rather than gating off, leaving a low idle drone.

LEVEL-START FANFARE, and the most elaborate sound in the cartridge.
fanfareCounter runs $30 down to 1; for each value, X counts the same value
down, and every step:
  FanfareSfxStep returns A = $40 - X, which is written to V1FREQHI,
  V2FREQHI and V3FREQHI - all three voices on the same coarse pitch;
  all three CTRL are gated off and then set to $25 =
  %00100101 = SAWTOOTH + RING MODULATION + gate.
Ring modulation multiplies a voice against its neighbours triangle, so
three ring-modulated saws at one pitch give the clangorous metallic
sweep you hear before a level. The outer loop shortens each sweep, so the
fanfare accelerates.
At the same time fanfareCounter is written straight into COLOUR RAM at
$D95E/$D95F, cycling the colour of the two grid-area digits on screen
in step with the sound - picture and sound driven by one counter.

PLAYER DEATH. All three voices are gated off, V1FREQHI is set to $03 and
from then on only voice 1 is used, retriggered as noise every frame at
$8B24 while SIGVOL is set to blastFrames - so the blast fades out as its
animation counts down. Eight fragments are seeded at the players cell and
blown outward. Char $16 is the blast glyph, drawn in ORANGE.

A droid that is NOT a squad leader (flag bit6 clear) copies the position of the droid one slot below it in the array - droidCol[X] = droidCol[X-1] - and draws itself in char $13. That is the whole of the chain behaviour: only the leader is steered, and every follower is one step behind its predecessor, so the squad moves as a snake. The array order IS the chain order, which is why destroying a droid has to compact the array rather than leave a hole.

The leader. Direction is droidFlags bits 0/1; the step is written as INC INC DEC or INC DEC so the sign comes out of how many INCs are skipped, the same trick the death-explosion deltas use. Hitting row $16 (below the grid) wraps to row $0E and flips the direction bits.

Compact the droid arrays: shift every entry from X upward down by one and decrement droidCount. This is why droid identity is an array index and nothing else - there is no id, and a droid destroyed in the middle makes every droid above it change index. PromoteNewSquadLeader runs first so the leader bit is ORed into the survivor before the shuffle moves it.

Title-screen input, and it is a SECOND, independent piece of joystick code. It compares the raw $DC11 byte against $EF (fire, bit4 low) and $FE (up, bit0 low) - active low, where ReadJoystick $8373 inverts to active high. Two conventions in one program because the title screen predates or postdates the game loop; nothing shares.

Level-start fanfare: a descending two-tone sweep, $30 steps, while the two level digits at $055E/$055F flash by writing fanfareCounter straight into colour RAM at $D95E/$D95F. Falls through into StartLevel.
X starts at 0 from $8060 and at 1..6 from HighScoreNextDigit

Verified by execution: with screenPtr=$0400, Y=$0A, plotChar=$07, plotColour=$0D this block writes $07 to $040A and $0D to $D80A, and leaves screenPtr pointing at $D800. Every caller must go through ScreenPtrForPlotRow again - the pointer is destroyed by the call.

args.text:
CHARACTER GENERATOR BASE. $D018 = $18 puts the VIC screen at $0400 and the
character base here; CopyCharacterSet $82EC fills $2000-$21FF from
characterSetData $8E00. Only 64 glyphs exist, so nothing above screen code
$3F is ever legal.

EVERY GAME OBJECT IS A CHARACTER. There is not one sprite in Gridrunner:
no write to $D000-$D010, $D015, $D01D/$D017 or $07F8-$07FF exists anywhere
in the cartridge. The playfield IS the object list - collision is done by
ReadCharAtPlotPos $818B reading a screen cell back and comparing the glyph.

What each glyph is, and how it was established:
  $00  the grid cross. Drawn over the whole playfield by DrawGridWipe pass 2,
       and used as the ERASE character everywhere inside the grid - erasing
       means putting the grid back. Colour ORANGE.
  $01  left zapper, walks down column 0.   $02 bottom zapper, walks along row $16.
  $03 $04  sparks trailing the horizontal zapper beam (beamChar - 2).
  $05 $06  the zapper beam itself; beamChar cycles $05,$06 in WHITE.
  $07  THE PLAYER SHIP, LIGHT_GREEN. Tested by name at $8023, $8483, $877A,
       $87B4, $8AE9 - every one of those is "did something touch the player".
  $08 $09  the players laser, WHITE. laserChar counts $08,$09 and RESETS at
       $0A, so $0A is never drawn as a laser - which is exactly why
       DieUnlessHarmlessChar $8BEC forgives $08 and $09 and nothing else.
  $0A  a falling bomb, WHITE, drawn by MoveOneBomb $876C.
  $0D $0E $0F $10 $11 $12 $18  the droid/pod damage frames, in that order in
       droidAnimFrames $871F. A new one appears as $0F (yellow) where a droid
       dies and at the end of a zapper beam sweep; a laser hit steps it BACK
       one frame, so its frame number is its remaining hit points.
  $13 $14 $15  the snake segments, CYAN, one hit each. $14 and $15 score more
       than $13 (LaserHitOtherChar $8A11 gives them an extra AddToScore).
  $16 $17 $18  the explosion, WHITE. blastChar cycles $16,$17,$18 and the
       glyphs get sparser each frame, so the burst visibly thins as it fades.
  $19 $1A  a two-cell label on the status line before the score field.
  $1B $1C  the letter Y (two identical glyphs).
  $1D $1E  a two-cell "HI" before the high-score field.
  $1F  an up arrow.  $20 blank.  $3F the vertical bar used for the grid wipe.

Glyphs I could not attribute to any drawing site: $0B, $0C (a mirrored pair,
almost certainly the two zapper heads in their other orientation) and
$11, $12 which are in the droid table but which no code sets directly.
What would settle it: running the game, or a trace of plotChar values.

comments.text:
THE MAIN LOOP. Three addresses form one cycle: MainLoopTop $83A0 jumps here; here calls UpdatePlayer and PauseOnKeyP and jumps to MainLoopUpdates $83A3, which calls nine update routines and jumps to MainLoopDelay $83E8, which burns 21 iterations of DEX and jumps back to MainLoopTop.

There is no interrupt and no raster sync anywhere in the program. The NMI vector is a bare RTI, no IRQ vector is ever installed ($0314 is never written), and $D01A is never touched. The loop free-runs, so the game's speed is whatever this code happens to take, and every subsystem is paced by counting loop iterations rather than frames.

Two counters do the pacing, and the trick is that different subsystems test them at DIFFERENT values, so the work spreads out instead of all landing on one iteration:

  tick $0D - UpdatePlayer decrements it. ReloadTickIfWrapped $89A0 puts it back to $80 the moment it reads $FF, so the cycle is 128 iterations long.
    == 0  UpdatePlayer moves the player
    == 1  UpdateZappers runs (and then halves itself again with zapperStepDelay)
    odd   ExplosionSfxStep runs
    == $FF ReloadTickIfWrapped resets it

  phase $0F - UpdateLaser decrements it and reloads it to $18, so 24 iterations.
    == 0  UpdateLaser steps the shot
    == 5  FireZapperBeam fires, and NextBeamChar $86D0 decrements phase a SECOND time while a beam is running, which is how the beam gets several iterations out of one slot.

So `CMP #$05 / BEQ` at the top of a routine is not a magic number, it is a time slot, and phase is decremented from two places.

The laser hit something that is not in droidAnimFrameTable, so not a droid in its damage animation. Three characters are worth points and everything else is ignored - the shot passes straight through a zapper glyph or another bomb.

  $13 -> +100   (a chain follower; every non-leader droid draws itself as $13)
  $14 -> +400   (a leader; droidChar cycles $13,$14,$15 at $88DA)
  $15 -> +400

The arithmetic: AddToScore takes X = digit position within scoreDigits, 0 being the most significant of seven, and Y = how many times to increment it. X=4 is the hundreds column, so Y=3 at $8A21 is +300 and it then falls through into $8A28 for another +100. Compare ScoreDroidKill, which uses X=6 Y=$0A - ten increments of the units column, i.e. +10 for finishing off a damaged droid.

This routine also discards its own return address at $8A33 (PLA PLA), like LaserHitsChar, and then walks the droid array at $8A37 to find and remove whatever it just shot.

tick has wrapped past 0 to $FF; put it back to $80. This is the only thing that ever writes tick apart from UpdatePlayer's DEC, and it is what makes the player's movement period 128 loop iterations rather than 256.

Advance the beam character and - the part that matters - decrement `phase` a second time. FireZapperBeam only runs when phase is exactly 5, so without this the beam would get one iteration per 24; with it, the beam holds the slot by pushing phase along itself.
X = digit column, 0 = millions, 6 = units; Y = how many increments
+300, then falls through for +100 more
+10: ten increments of the units digit
Score and make the explosion noise. Sets the sfxFreq sweep that ExplosionSfxStep plays out over the following iterations, then tail-calls AddToScore with whatever X and Y the caller set.

The level-start materialise effect: five characters walked outward from the centre of the grid (column $14, row $15) in a diamond, with fxCounter as the radius, counting down from $0F while the SID sweeps. ExplodeOutwardsStep $8264 draws one radius, ExplodeOutwardsNext $8400 erases it and either steps the radius or, at the end, draws the ship and plays three descending SweepDownSfx bursts. The three pieces are separate addresses only because the effect jumps between them rather than looping.

Draw the grid, as an animation rather than a fill. First pass: for each column 2..$26 draw a bar ($3F) down rows 2..$15, with a note of the SID sweeping as the column advances. Second pass: for each row 2..$15 overwrite columns 1..$26 with the empty cell $00, again with sound. So the grid is drawn and then wiped to the playing field, and what you actually see is a sweep left-to-right and then top-to-bottom.

Note $81D7/$81D8 and $820C/$820D: DEY / BNE to the very next instruction. The branch cannot go anywhere useful whichever way it falls - it is a two-byte no-op that only wastes time, i.e. hand-tuned delay.

Draw the 40-character status line and its colours from statusLineCharTable / statusLineColourTable. The loop runs X = $28 down to 1 over `table-1`, so its last fetch is one byte PAST the end of the character table - which is $8847, the first byte of the colour table, $34 = the character 4. That is where the initial four lives comes from: it is the first colour byte, read as a character, because the two tables are adjacent. ResetScoreAndLives $80E5 writes the same $34 explicitly, so whether the overrun is deliberate or a coincidence that happens to work cannot be settled from the code alone.

args.name: lead-structure
args.note: Control flow, routine names, zero-page map, level tables and dead-code archaeology all in. Zero unexplained bytes.

comments.text:
Written once, at $83C5: SCROLX = $05 = %00000101.
Bit 3 clear selects 38-COLUMN MODE, and bits 0-2 set a horizontal scroll of
5 pixels. Nothing ever writes it again, so this is the display for the whole
game - it is not scrolling, it is a fixed narrower window.
The consequence is that the border eats into the two extreme character
columns, and both are used: column 0 is the track the left zapper walks down
($85AA sets plotCol = 0) and column 39 holds the lives digit ($0427).
I cannot say from the code alone how much of either survives the border -
that is a pixel question, not a byte question. What would settle it: running
the cartridge, or a raster-accurate screenshot. Worth settling, because if
column 39 is covered then the lives count is invisible.

Written once, at $810B, and only ever $18 = %00011000:
  bits 4-7 = %0001 -> video matrix at $0400
  bits 1-3 = %100  -> character generator at $2000, the games own font
Written through STA ($02),Y with $02/$03 = $D000 and Y = $18, so the value
stored is the same number as the register offset. That is why a search for
absolute stores into the VIC range finds almost nothing.

Border and background are both set to $00, BLACK, once at $8111/$8114 and
never touched again. Gridrunner does no border flashing and no raster
effects at all: there is no interrupt handler except the do-nothing NMI at
$83E2, and $D011/$D012 are never read or written. Every visible change in
the game is a character or a colour-RAM byte.

Volume and filter select. The filter bits (4-7) are always 0 here, and
$D415-$D417 are never written, so the filter is unused. The low nibble is
worked as a fader: $8414 writes $0F - fxCounter, $8B30 writes blastFrames,
and $842D/$8437/$843F step $0F, $08, $02 through three chirps.

UPDATE DROIDS. Runs once per $80 loop iterations, the same rate as the player.

Three parallel arrays indexed 1..droidCount, all addressed as table-1,X: droidCol $1100, droidRow $1200, droidFlags $1300.

droidFlags is two markers and a direction, and getting these right is what explains the game:
  bit6 ($40) - HEAD of a chain. Only a head is steered; everyone else follows.
  bit7 ($80) - TAIL of a chain. Only a tail is erased.
  bits 0/1   - the head's direction, flipped with EOR #$03 at $8962.

The chain runs from low index (head) to high index (tail), because SpawnDroids appends. A follower at index X simply copies the position of index X-1, one place ahead of it. So the update per step is: erase the tail cell, copy every position along by one, move the head. That is a snake, done in four instructions, and it is why there is no per-droid velocity anywhere.

A head that reaches row $16 - below the grid - is put back to row $0E and has its direction bits forced, which is the drop-a-row-and-reverse sweep.

Plot only if droidFlags bit7 is set, i.e. only if this droid is the TAIL of its chain. The caller has already loaded the erase character, so this is the tail-erase half of the snake update. A droid in the middle is never erased because the droid behind it is about to draw over its cell anyway.

A follower: copy the position of the droid one index ahead - droidCol[X] = droidCol[X-1], droidRow[X] = droidRow[X-1] - and draw it as char $13. This is the entire follow behaviour, and it is why the array order IS the chain order and why removing a droid has to compact rather than leave a hole.

A droid in the MIDDLE of a chain was destroyed - neither head (bit6) nor tail (bit7). Splitting the chain in two is what happens next, and it is the most interesting thing in the program.

Scan down from X until a droid with bit6 is found: that is the head of this chain, and its flags carry the direction. OR those flags into index X+1, so the droid behind the gap becomes a head in its own right, travelling the same way. Then OR $80 into index X-1, so the droid in front of the gap becomes a tail.

One chain in, two chains out, each with its own head and tail, sharing one array. Shooting the middle of a squad does not shorten it - it doubles the number of things chasing you.

Which repair is needed depends on what the destroyed droid was:
  neither bit ($00) - a middle droid: PromoteNewSquadLeader splits the chain
  both bits ($C0)   - a chain of one: nothing to repair
  bit6 only ($40)   - the head: OR its flags into X+1, which inherits the lead and the direction
  bit7 only ($80)   - the tail: OR $80 into X-1, which becomes the new tail
Only then is the array compacted.

SPAWN, one droid per call. A wave is a head followed by droidsPerWave-1 followers, all created at column $0A row $02 - the top of the grid - and appended to the arrays.

  waveRemaining != 0 : append a follower with flags $00. The one that takes waveRemaining to 1 gets flags $80 (tail), and wavesLeft is decremented - a wave counts as spent when it is fully spawned, not when it is destroyed.
  waveRemaining == 0 : count spawnCountdown down from $20 and, if wavesLeft is not 0, start the next wave with a head, flags $41 = bit6 plus direction 1.

Both wavesLeft and droidsPerWave come out of levelParameterTables, so the level number controls how many chains there are and how long each one is. Nothing else about a level changes except the zapper interval.

ANIMATE DROIDS - and it is a screen scan, not an object loop. Every $05 of zapperFireCountdown it walks scanPtr from $0450 to $07FF, one byte at a time, and any character it finds in droidAnimFrameTable it advances to the next frame. A droid on the last frame ($12) calls DroidDropsBomb.

So the animation state of a droid is not in any array: it IS the character code sitting in screen memory. Damage works the same way - LaserHitsChar walks the same table backwards. The screen is the model, and the arrays hold only what the screen cannot: position history for the chain and the flag bits.

Two details worth knowing. The scan starts at $0450, which is row 2 column 0 - the top of the grid, deliberately below the status line. It ends when the pointer's high byte reaches $08, so it runs to $07FF, which is 24 bytes PAST the end of the 1000-byte screen at $07E7. Those bytes are the sprite pointer area; nothing writes them and nothing there matches the table, so the overrun is harmless, but it is an overrun.

The whole of the difficulty curve, decoded (level: waves x droids-per-wave, zapper interval):

  1: 1x6/16   2: 2x6/16   3: 2x6/16   4: 3x7/15   5: 3x7/14   6: 3x8/13
  7: 4x8/12   8: 4x9/11   9: 4x12/10 10: 4x12/9  11: 5x10/9  12: 5x10/9
 13: 16x3/9  14: 6x15/9  15: 6x16/9  16: 6x16/9  17: 6x17/8  18: 6x18/8
 19: 6x19/8  20: 6x20/8  21: 6x20/7  22: 6x20/7  23: 6x21/7  24: 6x21/7
 25: 6x22/7  26: 6x22/7  27: 7x22/7  28: 7x23/7  29: 7x3/7   30: 7x24/6
 31: 7x24/6  32: 7x25/5

Two entries are outliers and I cannot tell from the code which they are. Level 13 is 16 waves of 3 where its neighbours are 5-6 waves of 10-15: both of its numbers jump at once, which is what a transposed pair of bytes looks like, but 48 short chains is also a perfectly good boss level. Level 29 is 7 waves of 3 where its neighbours are 22 and 24 droids, which reads as a breather - except that a breather two levels from the end is odd. args.description:
Gridrunner (Jeff Minter, HES, 1982), the 4K C64 cartridge, loaded at $8000-$8FFF.

A CBM80 autostart cartridge: $8000-$8008 is a vector table, not code, and execution begins at ColdStart $83C1. $8E00-$8FFF is a 64-character font that is copied to $2000 before anything else runs; the whole game is drawn with those characters and there are no sprites.

Shape of the program:
  ColdStart $83C1 -> CopyCharsetToRam $82EC -> InitVicSidAndScreen $8100 -> DrawStatusLine $8806 -> TitleScreen $8D8E
  TitleScreen: joystick up picks a level 1..32, fire starts -> ResetScoreAndLives $80E5 -> NewLevel $8C2D
  NewLevel -> LevelStartFanfare $8D16 -> StartLevel $8300 -> MainLoop $8393
  MainLoop: UpdatePlayer, PauseOnKeyP, then nine updates at $83A3, then a delay, forever
  PlayerDies $8ADE resets the stack -> PlayerDeathExplosion $8AF8 -> LoseALife $8C17 -> RestartSameLevel or CheckHighScore $8060 -> TitleScreen
  WaveClearedCheck $8AC8 is the only other way out of the loop: it jumps to NewLevel

There is no interrupt anywhere. No IRQ vector is installed, the NMI vector is a bare RTI so RESTORE does nothing, and everything is paced by counting main-loop iterations against two counters, `tick` (period 128) and `phase` (period 24), with different subsystems testing them at different values.

The screen is the model. Collision is done by reading the character already in the cell being moved into; a droid s damage state is the character code on screen and nothing else; the score, the high score and the number of lives are digits in screen memory at $040F, $041B and $0427, with no binary copy anywhere. Everything drawn goes through PlotCharAndColour $8172.

Of 4096 bytes, none are unexplained. About 110 bytes are unreachable: NOP padding, four little routines with no callers, and - the interesting one - the tail of the charset-copy loop at $8009, left stranded when the CBM80 header was placed over the top of its first nine bytes.

args.text:
beryl: taken, sound and glyphs are yours. Two corrections back and one thing you will want.

* Your $8C61 is $8C62 (the LDA is `BD 62 8C`), and your " BATTLE  STATIONS " is 18 bytes from $8C51, which is what I declared. Your $8848/40-bytes for the colour table is right about what is USED; I declared the region from $8847 because the char loop reads that byte as its X=$28 entry - which is where the initial 4 lives comes from. Both statements are true of different byte ranges, so neither region is wrong.

* Things I established that touch your side: there are exactly three VIC writes in the program and constant folding resolves all of them ($D018=$18, $D020=$00, $D021=$00, all through the $02/$03 pointer at $8100). $D015, $D01A and $0314 are never written - I checked as byte patterns, not just as decoded instructions. So no sprites, no raster interrupt, no IRQ at all: the game is one free-running loop and every sound you find is triggered by a counter comparison, not by a timer.

* The two counters, since every sound routine is gated on one: `tick` $0D has period 128 (UpdatePlayer decrements, ReloadTickIfWrapped $89A0 resets it to $80 at $FF) and `phase` $0F has period 24 (UpdateLaser decrements and reloads $18). Routines test them at specific VALUES, not for zero - CMP #$05 / BEQ at the top of a routine means "my time slot", not a magic constant. NextBeamChar $86D0 decrements phase a second time while a beam is running, which is how the beam holds its slot.

* Still open on my side and it is yours if you want it: char $13/$14/$15 are the droid glyphs (droidChar cycles them at $88DA) and hitting $13 with the laser scores 100 while $14/$15 score 400. I have not worked out why the leader is worth four times a follower when they are the same object.

comments.text:

The curve, level: waves x droids-per-wave, zapper fire interval:

  1: 1x6/16   2: 2x6/16   3: 2x6/16   4: 3x7/15   5: 3x7/14   6: 3x8/13
  7: 4x8/12   8: 4x9/11   9: 4x12/10 10: 4x12/9  11: 5x10/9  12: 5x10/9

cap: $20 is pushed back to $1F, so 31 is the last level
a free life per level, capped at 9

Unreachable. This is entry $20 of levelZapperInterval, and `level` is capped at $1F, so nothing ever indexes here. The corresponding entries of the other two tables ($8CD4, $8CF4) are unreachable for the same reason but are doing double duty as the next table's base; this byte is not.
only caller is BootDrawStatusLine, so the high score survives a game

Glyphs $0B and $0C, and they are DEAD ART. They are exact horizontal
mirrors of one another (00 C0 72 1F 1F 72 C0 00 against
00 03 4E F8 F8 4E 03 00 - every byte bit-reversed), a left- and
right-facing pair. Nothing draws them: find_immediates says neither $0B
nor $0C is ever loaded anywhere in the cartridge, they are not in
droidAnimFrames, and they appear in none of the five character tables
($8080, $8820, $8C51, $8DE1, $871F). Every other glyph is reachable.
My guess is a discarded pair of horizontal enemies; that is a guess, and
what would settle it is an earlier build, not this binary.

Glyphs $1B and $1C are the letter Y, and they are BYTE-IDENTICAL:
both C6 C6 00 7C 38 38 38 38. Only $1B is used - "BY JEFF MINTER" at
$8DE1 begins 29 1B. $1C is a duplicate nothing refers to.
Worth noticing because it is the only letter in the font that appears
twice, which is what you would expect if the alphabet was packed by hand
in the order it was needed and one letter got added twice.

Glyph $1F, an up arrow, drawn by nothing. Like $0B/$0C it is never loaded
and appears in no character table. Together with $0B, $0C and the
duplicate $1C, four of the 64 glyphs are unreachable - about 6% of the
font is left-over or spare art.

droidCol minus two. The droid arrays are one-based - element n lives at droidCol+n - so the code addresses them as droidCol-1,X. This label exists because reading the droid ONE PLACE AHEAD in the chain needs droidCol-2,X, and a -2 offset is beyond what the disassembler will fold into a neighbouring name (it renders table-1 and no further). Naming the address is the honest way to say it.

Clear the playfield: fill $0450-$07FF with $20. Note this leaves row 0 ($0400-$0427) alone, which is why the score, the high score and the lives digit survive it - they ARE row 0.

It uses $07/$08 as its pointer, which are screenPtr+1 and gridCol everywhere else in the program. Nothing is corrupted because it is only called between frames, but the second reading is real and is bound here as clearPtrLo/clearPtrHi.

Like AnimateDroidsOnScreen it stops when the high byte reaches $08, so it writes 24 bytes past the end of the 1000-byte screen, into the sprite pointer area. Harmless in a game with no sprites.
entered with X=0; HighScoreNextDigit re-enters the loop with X=1..6

The first digit that differs decides it. CMP has already run, so N is set if the score digit is LOWER than the high-score digit - BMI means no record. Falling through means higher, so copy all seven digits across. Reaching the end of the loop without a difference means equal, which also counts as no record.

The laser hit a droid, but the character on the screen does not say WHICH array entry it was - the arrays are the only place a droid's identity lives. So walk droidCol/droidRow from droidCount down looking for the entry whose position matches, and that is the one to remove. Linear, and it runs once per hit, so at most 25 comparisons.

One frame of the death explosion, repeated 15 times (blastFrames). Each frame: erase every fragment cell that still holds the PREVIOUS blast character - the CMP blastChar at $8B4C is what stops the explosion scribbling over droids or the grid - then advance blastChar ($16,$17,$18 cycling), move all eight fragments outward by their delta vectors, and draw them. A fragment that walks off the grid is reset to the player's last position by StepFragCol/StepFragRow, so the burst folds back on itself rather than escaping.

Print the two level banners: "BATTLE STATIONS" at $04FE in light blue and "ENTER GRID AREA 00" at $054E in white. Both tables are indexed one-based from a base that is the last byte of the preceding instruction, the same byte-saving trick the level tables use.

Busy-wait. Two nested loops of DEC delayCounter / BNE from 0, so 256 x 256 iterations - about a third of a second. This and the DEX/BNE at MainLoopDelay are the only timing in the program; there is no raster wait anywhere.
Delay, but only if fxCounter is non-zero - so the sound effects that use fxCounter as a radius get shorter as the effect converges, without the caller having to say so.

comments.text:
CLI, and this needs saying because it is easy to conclude the opposite. The game installs no interrupt handler of its own - $0314 is never written and $D01A is never touched - but it does NOT run with interrupts off. JSR ROM_RESTOR at $83CE puts the KERNAL's default vectors back and IOINIT has already enabled CIA1 timer A, so from this instruction on the ordinary 60Hz KERNAL IRQ is running underneath the whole game.

That matters for two reasons. It is what keeps $C5 (the currently-pressed key) updated, which is the only reason PauseOnKeyP works at all - nothing in this program scans the keyboard. And it means the game is not free of interrupts, it is merely not SYNCHRONISED to them: the main loop never waits for anything and the KERNAL IRQ steals time from it at unpredictable points.

These two instructions - here and the identical one at $8DB0 - are the ONLY reads of anything in the I/O page in the entire program. Verified with find_instructions over $D000-$DFFF for LDA: two hits, both this. No raster register is read, no SID oscillator, no CIA timer, no jiffy clock.

The consequence is worth stating plainly: Gridrunner has no source of randomness. Droid spawn positions are fixed at column $0A row $02, wave sizes come out of a table, the zappers sweep on a fixed period, and the beams fire on a per-level interval. Given the same starting level and the same joystick inputs, the game plays out identically every time.

Pause on P. $C5 is the KERNAL's current-key-pressed byte and $29 is the matrix code for P; the game never scans the keyboard itself, it reads what the KERNAL IRQ has already put there.

The sequence is deliberately four-stage and reads oddly: return if P is not down; wait for it to be released; wait for it to be pressed again; then WaitKeyPRelease. So the first press pauses and holds, and the second press resumes. Both edges are waited for, which is what stops one long press toggling the pause dozens of times.

Note $821F BNE goes to the RTS at $821A, which is UpdateZappers' RTS. Two routines sharing an RTS to save a byte.

args.text:
Correction to something I said earlier and to anything you have written that follows it: the game is NOT running with interrupts disabled. ColdStart does SEI, then JSR ROM_RESTOR ($FD15) which puts the KERNAL default vectors back, then CLI at $83D4. IOINIT has already enabled CIA1 timer A. So the ordinary 60Hz KERNAL IRQ runs underneath the whole game.

What is true is that the game installs nothing of its own ($0314 never written, $D01A never written) and never waits for anything. So it is unsynchronised, not uninterrupted - and the KERNAL IRQ is the only reason $C5 is up to date, which is the only reason the P-key pause works, since nothing here scans the keyboard.

Separately, and it may matter for how you read the sound: I searched every LDA over $D000-$DFFF and there are exactly two, both `LDA $DC11` (the joystick, at $8373 and $8DB0). Nothing reads a raster line, a SID oscillator, a CIA timer or the jiffy clock. There is no randomness anywhere in this program - spawn position is a constant, wave sizes are a table, the zappers are periodic. Same level plus same inputs gives the same game every time.

$19 $1A - the two-cell label in front of the SCORE field, and the one thing
on this screen I could not read.

Evidence for what it labels: scoreDigits is $040F-$0415 (columns 15-21) and
hiScoreDigits is $041B-$0421 (columns 27-33), confirmed by AddToScore $8870
and CheckHighScore $8055. These two cells sit at columns 12-13, one blank

The pixels, both cells side by side:

  ##.##.##......##
  ####..##......##
  ##....##......##
  ##....####.##.##
Compare $1D $1E, which parses cleanly as H(6px) I(4px) colon(3px):

comments.text:
THE CHARACTER SET: 64 glyphs, 8 bytes each, copied to $2000 by
CopyCharsetToRam. It is a CUSTOM font, so no built-in PETSCII or
screen-code table reads it. Mapping, read off the bitmaps and confirmed
by decoding four strings:

  $20 space
  $21 G  $22 R  $23 U  $24 I  $25 D  $26 N  $27 E  $28 A  $29 B
  $2A F  $2B H  $2C J  $2D M  $2E P  $2F S

character tables ($8080, $8820, $8C51, $8DE1, $871F).

reaches it by adding $D4 to the screen pointers high byte, which is why a

pointer (the two title strings, BATTLE STATIONS, the fanfare colour cycle
and MoveOneBomb).

The whole palette the game uses, and what each colour means. Bit 4 of
$D016 is clear and $D011 is left as CINT set it, so this is hires text:
one colour per character, on black.

  $01 WHITE        the zappers, the zapper beam, the players laser,

                   "ENTER LEVEL" / "ENTER GRID AREA" lines
  $03 CYAN         the score digits, the snake segments, "BY JEFF MINTER",

  $04 PURPLE       the letters RUNNER, and the lives digit

  $0D LIGHT_GREEN  the player ship, and only the player ship
  $0E LIGHT_BLUE   the hi-score digits and "BATTLE STATIONS"
Seven colours and black. No multicolour, no raster splits, no colour
cycling except the one in LevelStartFanfare $8D16, which writes a counter
straight into $D95E/$D95F so the two grid-area digits change colour in
step with the sound.

Sound is done and in the project. Headlines:

- 66 stores into $D400-$D418, and the registers the game NEVER writes are the story: no FREQLO on any voice, no pulse width, no filter at all. Pitch is the HIGH BYTE only - 256 coarse steps. Everything is done inline in the game loop; there is no interrupt and no music.

Voice 3 is the only pitched one: SAWTOOTH ($21) for the zapper beam and the explosion sweep, and RING-MODULATED sawtooth ($25) for the level-start fanfare, which runs all three voices at one pitch. comments.text: $04xx screen -> $D8xx colour RAM. Verified by running this block: with screenPtr=$0640, Y=$14, plotChar=$07, plotColour=$0D it wrote $07 to $0654 and $0D to $DA54.

NOTHING IN THIS GAME IS SYNCHRONISED TO THE RASTER. $D011 and $D012 are
never read or written, the IRQ vector at $0314 is never touched, and the
only interrupt entry is the NMI stub at $83E2 that does nothing. Every
character is poked straight into $0400 whenever the game loop gets round to
it, so the picture tears by design and the frame rate is whatever the code
happens to take. That is also why the sound has to be driven inline, one
register write at a time, from the same loop that draws.

FIRE ZAPPER BEAM, and it does more than kill: it is where new droids come from once a level is under way.

Runs only when phase is 5 AND beamActive is $FF (armed by UpdateZappers). NextBeamChar advances beamChar and also decrements phase again, which is how the beam keeps its own slot for several iterations. beamChar cycles $05/$06, wrapping at $07 - the CMP #$07 at $8646 is that wrap, NOT a test for the ship glyph, which is what it looks like at a glance and what I bound a constant to before reading it properly.

Each pass:
1. Redraw the vertical beam in white down column beamVertCol from row $15 up to row 3.
2. At (beamCol, beamRow), read the cell. If it already holds beamChar the horizontal sweep has caught up with itself and the beam is over.
3. Otherwise erase that cell, advance beamCol, and look at the new one with CharIsPlayerThenDie - which is where the beam kills.
4. Draw the leading edge. Note $869A: CLC then SBC #$01, so the glyph is beamChar MINUS TWO, not minus one.

EraseZapperBeam $86A2 then clears the vertical line back to grid cells - and drops a droid glyph $0F, in yellow, at (beamVertCol, beamRow): the intersection of the two beams. plotCol is still the vertical beam column at that point, which is easy to misread as a leftover. So the two edge zappers firing across each other is not just a hazard, it seeds a new droid where they cross, and AnimateDroidsOnScreen picks that glyph up on its next scan and starts animating it. That is the feedback loop that keeps a level populated after the spawn waves are spent.
CLC before SBC: this is beamChar - 2

CLC before SBC, and the program does this EVERYWHERE. There are six real `CLC / SBC` sites - $8278, $828C, $82C9, $82E4, $8411 and $869A - and not one `SEC / SBC` anywhere in the 4K. On a 6502 SBC subtracts the carry's complement, so a cleared carry takes an extra 1: every subtraction in this program is one less than it reads.

Proved rather than argued: running the block at $8264 with fxCounter = $0F leaves plotCol = $04. $14 - $0F is $05. The effect is one column further left than the arithmetic says.

All six sites are inside visual effects - the materialise diamond, the volume ramp, the beam glyph - where being one out is invisible, which is presumably why it survived. It is worth knowing before anyone tries to reproduce the geometry of the level-start effect and finds it will not line up.

args.text:
Two findings that change how the game reads, both now in comments.

1. FireZapperBeam $8635 does not only kill. When the sweep finishes, EraseZapperBeam $86A2 drops a droid glyph $0F in yellow at (beamVertCol, beamRow) - the point where the two zapper beams cross - and AnimateDroidsOnScreen picks it up on its next scan and starts animating it. So the zappers seed new droids where they intersect. That is the feedback loop that keeps a level populated after the spawn waves are spent, and it explains why the beams fire more often on later levels (levelZapperInterval falls from 16 to 6).

2. The program never uses SEC before SBC. Six real sites - $8278, $828C, $82C9, $82E4, $8411, $869A - all CLC/SBC, zero SEC/SBC in the whole 4K. So every subtraction is one less than it reads. Proved by running the block at $8264 with fxCounter=$0F: plotCol comes out $04, where $14-$0F is $05. All six are inside visual or volume effects where one out is invisible, which is presumably why nobody noticed. Relevant to you if you try to reproduce the materialise geometry or the volume ramp at $8411 ($0F CLC SBC fxCounter -> SIGVOL).

Also a correction to myself: I had bound CHAR_SHIP to the CMP #$07 at $8646. It is not the ship, it is the beamChar wrap. Unbound.

agate: we have collided on constants - the equate block now carries CHAR_EMPTY and GLYPH_GRID for $00, CHAR_SHIP and GLYPH_SHIP for $07, CHAR_SPACE and GLYPH_BLANK for $20. I have merged my side into yours for $07 and $20 and deleted GLYPH_SHIP and GLYPH_BLANK.

For $00 I would rather keep GLYPH_GRID and drop CHAR_EMPTY, and the reason is a finding rather than taste: $00 is not blank. It is the cross that DrawGridWipe pass 2 paints over the whole playfield, and it is used as the erase character everywhere inside the grid precisely because erasing there means putting the grid back. $20 is the genuinely empty cell and is only used outside the grid, on the zapper tracks. Naming $00 "empty" hides the nicest thing about the drawing code. Your call - if you rebind CHAR_EMPTY sites I will drop GLYPH_GRID instead, but one of the two should go.

Note how this happened: neither of us had a way to see the other declaring a name for the same byte value. list_constants exists but you would only call it if you already suspected. That is the same shape as the two charset decoders.

comments.text:
THE POD LIFE CYCLE, which is the game's central mechanic and is entirely encoded in this nine-byte table.

There are two enemy types and they are represented completely differently:

  CHAIN DROIDS - glyphs $13 (segment) and $14/$15 (head). They live in the droidCol/droidRow/droidFlags arrays, move as snakes, are created by SpawnDroids from the level tables, and die in one laser hit.

  PODS - glyphs $18, $0D, $0E, $0F, $10, $11, $12, in that order, which is this table read from index 1 to 7. A pod is held NOWHERE except as a character on the screen: no array, no coordinates, no id. AnimateDroidsOnScreen finds it by scanning the whole playfield and advances it one frame.

A pod ages forward $18 -> $0D -> ... -> $12, and at $12 DroidDropsBomb turns the cell into a bomb ($0A) and hands the screen address to a bomb slot. A laser hit steps it BACKWARD, one frame per hit, and destroying it at $18 scores 10.

Where pods come from is the part worth knowing. Glyph $0F - four frames into the sequence, so four hits from death - is written by exactly two instructions in the program:

  $86C5, in EraseZapperBeam: at the point where the two zapper beams cross.
  $8A71, in CompactDroidArrays: at the cell of a chain droid you just shot.

So killing a chain segment does not remove it, it leaves a pod behind that will grow and bomb you; and the zappers manufacture pods every time they fire. Both routes make more work than they remove, which is why the level parameter that rises fastest is how often the zappers fire.

Index 0 ($EA) and index 8 ($13) are never read by any of the three loops over this table. $13 being just past the end, and being the chain-segment glyph, is a coincidence worth noticing and not reading anything into: LaserHitOtherChar handles $13 with its own CMP.

The droid is gone from the arrays - now leave a POD in its place. Glyph $0F in yellow at plotCol/plotRow, which still hold the position FindDroidAtPlotPos matched. $0F is four frames into droidAnimFrameTable, so the pod needs four more laser hits and will drop a bomb if you leave it.

This is why shooting a chain is not obviously progress, and it is the difference between this game and a shooting gallery.

A pod has reached the last animation frame: turn it into a falling bomb. Write glyph $0A over the pod's cell, then scan bombPtrHi from slot 24 down for the $FF free marker and store the pod's screen pointer there - the bomb inherits the pod's position directly, with no coordinate conversion, because both are just a screen address.

If no slot is free the cell is written back as $12 instead, so the pod stays at the last frame and the next scan tries again. The cap is 24 bombs in flight and the failure mode is a delay, not a lost bomb.
a new pod, four frames from death, where the droid was
a new pod at the beam intersection

args.text:
Found the thing the whole game turns on, and I had it wrong twice before this. There are TWO enemy types with completely different representations.

CHAIN DROIDS: glyphs $13 (segment) / $14-$15 (head). Live in the droidCol/droidRow/droidFlags arrays at $1100/$1200/$1300, move as snakes (a follower copies the position of the entry one ahead), die in one hit. Shooting the middle of a chain SPLITS it into two chains ($8AA4) rather than shortening it.

PODS: glyphs $18, $0D, $0E, $0F, $10, $11, $12 - which is droidAnimFrameTable $871F read from index 1 to 7. A pod exists ONLY as a character on the screen. No array, no coordinates, no id. AnimateDroidsOnScreen $86D7 finds them by scanning $0450-$07FF and advancing each one a frame; at $12 it becomes a falling bomb; a laser hit steps it BACKWARD one frame, so a pod takes several hits.

And the connection: glyph $0F, four frames from death, is written by exactly two instructions in the whole cartridge. $86C5, where the two zapper beams cross. And $8A71, at the cell of a chain droid you just shot. So killing a droid leaves a pod, and the zappers manufacture pods every time they fire. The game gets harder by making more work than you remove, and the level parameter that changes fastest is how often the zappers fire.

beryl - your GLYPH_DROID_NEW for $0F is a good name and I have left it. GLYPH_SEGMENT_A for $13 is right too; $14/$15 are the same object animating, they are what droidChar cycles at $88DA.

SCREEN RAM, and the whole geometry of the game, derived from the drawing
loops rather than from any table:

  row  0   the status line. Copied from statusLineChars $881F and
           statusLineColours $8847 by DrawStatusLine $8806, 40 cells:
           GRIDRUNNER (cols 0-9), a two-cell label (12-13), the score

           (27-33), the ship glyph (36) and the lives digit $0427 (39).

  rows 2-21, cols 1-38   THE GRID. DrawGridWipe $81A2 pass 2 fills exactly
           this rectangle with glyph $00 in ORANGE. Pass 1, the visible
           wipe, covers cols 2-38 only - column 1 gets a cross but never a
           bar, which is a real off-by-one you can see if you look for it.
  rows 15-21, cols 1-38   the players box. UpdatePlayer clamps plotRow to

           bottom seven rows of the grid.
  col  0,  rows 3-21      the left zappers track, glyph $01.
  row  22, cols 1-38      the bottom zappers track, glyph $02.
  row  23  never written.

The row bases are NOT computed with a multiply: InitVicSidClearScreen
$8100 builds a 24-entry split table at screenRowLo $0340 and screenRowHi
$0360, and SetScreenPtrFromRowCol $8163 indexes it. Everything else in the
game reaches the screen through that.

And the screen is the game state. There is no object list to test against:
ReadCharAtPlotPos $818B reads a cell back and the glyph found there IS the
answer - so the bombs, the beams, the droids and the player all collide by
looking at what is drawn. Bombs are even stored as raw screen pointers
(bombPtrLo/bombPtrHi) rather than as coordinates, so falling one row is
adding 40.

$8100 builds a 24-entry split table at screenRowLo $0340 and screenRowHi
$0360, and SetScreenPtrFromRowCol $8163 indexes it. Everything else in the
