And the screen is the game state. There is no object list to test against:
ReadCharAtPlotPos $818B reads a cell back and the glyph found there IS the
answer - so the bombs, the beams, the droids and the player all collide by
looking at what is drawn. Bombs are even stored as raw screen pointers
(bombPtrLo/bombPtrHi) rather than as coordinates, so falling one row is
adding 40. The score is the same trick: AddToScore $8870 increments the
digit CHARACTERS at $040F, so there is no binary score anywhere in the
cartridge - the number on the screen is the number.

UPDATE PLAYER, and the sole reader of the joystick. Runs when tick reaches 0 - which is once per 128 main-loop iterations, because ReloadTickIfWrapped puts tick back to $80 as soon as it wraps to $FF, not per 256.

Order matters and is worth reading carefully:
1. Look at the cell the player is standing in. If it does not still hold the ship glyph, something has been drawn over the player since last time; DieUnlessHarmlessChar decides whether that is fatal.
2. Erase the old position to an empty grid cell.
3. Apply the joystick to plotCol/plotRow. Columns clamp to 1..$26, rows to $0F..$15 - seven rows at the bottom of the grid, which is the band the player is confined to. The grid itself runs rows 2..$15, so the player can reach only the bottom third of it.
4. Look at the cell being moved INTO. If it is not empty, PlayerRanIntoChar.
5. Save the new position to playerCol/playerRow and draw the ship.

The clamping is written as "if it went one past, put it back", not as a test before moving, so plotRow/plotCol briefly hold an illegal coordinate inside this routine. Nothing reads them in between, but a reader tracing the bounds should not expect to find a comparison.

Note what is NOT here: there is no test of the fire button. Firing is UpdateLaser's business, on a different counter.

args.text:
Housekeeping, and one thing I would rather ask than just do.

We now have duplicate constant names for the same value in the same equate block: CHAR_EMPTY / GLYPH_GRID at $00, CHAR_SHIP / GLYPH_SHIP at $07, CHAR_LASER / GLYPH_LASER_A at $08, CHAR_BOMB / GLYPH_BOMB at $0A, CHAR_SPACE / GLYPH_BLANK at $20. That is not a conflict re64 can see - a constant declaration is just a name for a value and two are allowed on purpose - but a listing that prints both is worse than either.

Your GLYPH_ prefix is the better convention because it distinguishes a character code from a colour, a row and a delay, all of which share these small values. I have deleted the three of mine that ended up bound nowhere (CHAR_ZAPPER_LEFT, CHAR_ZAPPER_BOTTOM, CHAR_GRID_BAR) and left the rest alone rather than unbinding sites you have bound. If you want to take the remaining CHAR_* over to GLYPH_*, go ahead and I will not fight you for them - but I am not going to rebind sites out from under you unannounced, because the last thing either of us needs is a rebinding war neither can see happening.

What I keep: ROW_PLAYER_TOP/BOTTOM, ROW_BELOW_GRID, COL_RIGHT_EDGE, MAX_LEVEL, LASER_IDLE, SLOT_FREE, KEY_P, CHAR_ZERO, CHAR_NINE_PLUS_1. Those name coordinates, limits and sentinels rather than glyphs, so they do not collide with your scheme.

comments.text:
UPDATE LASER - the player's shot, and there is exactly one slot for it in the whole program. laserRow = $FF means nothing is in flight, and the fire button is only read when it is $FF, which is why pressing fire does nothing while a shot is on screen.

A shot is launched from the player's cell one row up (laserCol/laserRow from playerCol/playerRow, then DEC), with laserChar $08 and laserSfx $40.

Each step: look at the cell ahead. Anything that is neither empty nor the shot's own current glyph goes to LaserHitsChar. Then draw the shot and INC laserChar; the glyph alternates $08 and $09, and when the increment reaches $0A the shot moves up one row and laserChar goes back to $08. So the two glyphs are one cell's worth of animation and the shot advances a row every second step.

Reaching row 2 - the top of the grid - retires the shot by setting laserRow back to $FF. So does a hit: both exits of LaserHitsChar write $FF there before discarding their return address.

It also decrements `phase`, which is the counter FireZapperBeam is gated on, so the laser is the clock for the zapper beams as well as for itself.

comments.text:
V1AD is written ONCE, at $811B, and never again - and the same is true of
V1SR ($8123), V2AD ($811E) and V2SR ($8126). So voices 1 and 2 keep one
envelope for the entire game: attack 0, decay $A, sustain 0, release 0.
Everything they do afterwards is gate-off/gate-on, which retriggers that
envelope - a click.
Evidence: routine_effects on MainLoopTop $83A0 lists exactly nine I/O
registers among its 71 writes - V1FREQHI, V1CTRL, V2FREQHI, V2CTRL,
V3FREQHI, V3CTRL, V3AD, V3SR and SIGVOL. V1AD, V1SR, V2AD and V2SR are not
among them, and neither is any VIC register: once the game is running it
never touches the video chip again.

V3AD is the only envelope the game ever changes after start-up, and it does
it twice in StartLevel: $830C sets $04 and $8336 sets $0A. Voice 3 is the
pitched voice - the zapper beam, the explosion sweep, the fanfare - so it
is the one where the envelope is worth touching.

args.text:
OSC3/RANDOM, the standard C64 random-number source: read voice 3 while it
runs a noise waveform and you get a fresh byte every cycle. Gridrunner
NEVER READS IT. find_instructions over $D419-$D41C returns nothing, and
over $DC04-$DC07 (the CIA timers, the other usual source) nothing either.
That corroborates the note at ReadJoystick $8373: the game has no source of
randomness at all. Everything - droid spawn positions, wave timing, which
cell a bomb falls from - is a counter. It is also a missed opportunity that
is almost free here, because voice 3 is already running noise for most of
the game.

Done - all five CHAR_* glyph names are now GLYPH_*, with every site that was bound to them rebound first, so nothing fell back to a literal. GLYPH_GRID, GLYPH_SHIP, GLYPH_LASER_A, GLYPH_BOMB, GLYPH_BLANK. Your coordinate/limit/sentinel names are untouched.

One correction while I was in there: $8D52 was bound to CHAR_SPACE, but that LDA #$20 is FanfareDelays delay count, not a character - it goes to $8388, not to plotChar. Unbound. Worth flagging as the failure mode of this whole mechanism: bind_constant will happily accept any site loading the right value, and $20 is a space, a level cap and a delay in three different places in this program.

Also worth naming, since it is the tool gap under both of our collisions: there is no way to ask "where is this constant bound?". list_constants reports a uses count that is 1 for a name bound at thirteen sites and 1 for a name bound at one, so it cannot answer it either. I had to run find_immediates on each value and read the rendered operand text to find your bindings. Same shape as the decoder collision and the constant-name collision: the write side is complete and the who-else-touched-this side is not.

Wrapping up. Report is at experiments/03-collaboration/run/report-lead.md.

Where I got to: 0 unexplained bytes of 4096, every routine named, the frame loop and its two counters documented, both enemy models worked out, the level tables decoded to 31 levels (not 32 - the cap at $8C86 makes the last table entry unreachable), and the dead code at $8009 identified as the stranded tail of the charset-copy loop that the CBM80 header was written over.

The thing I would most want a second pair of eyes on, because I could not settle it from the code: levels 13 and 29 in the level tables are outliers (16x3 and 7x3 among neighbours of 5-6 waves and 20+ droids). Level 13 has BOTH numbers jump at once, which is what a transposed byte pair looks like, but it is also a perfectly reasonable boss level. Emulator or a second dump would decide it; reading will not.

Thanks for the split - it held, and the two corrections you made to me were both load-bearing.

WHAT THE SOUNDS ACTUALLY SOUND LIKE.
Only the FREQHI byte is ever written, so the 16-bit frequency is always a
multiple of 256. On a PAL C64 (clock 985248, 24-bit accumulator) one step
of FREQHI is 256 * 985248 / 16777216 = about 15.0 Hz, so a FREQHI of n is
roughly n * 15 Hz. That gives every effect in the game a number:

  voices 1 and 2 run NOISE, so for them this is timbre, not pitch - the
  noise clock rate, i.e. how bright the hiss is - while voice 3 runs
  sawtooth and its number really is a pitch.

  init $8116        V1FREQHI $0A ~ 150 Hz, V2FREQHI $05 ~ 75 Hz
  grid wipe $8240   V1FREQHI = gridCol, 2 to $26: ~30 Hz rising to ~570 Hz
                    over the width of the screen. One click per character.
  laser $8573       both voices sweep down from $40 (~960 Hz) to 0
  materialise $8450 V2FREQHI $18 down to 1, TRIANGLE: ~360 Hz falling to
                    ~15 Hz, three times, quieter each time
  zapper beam $862F V3FREQHI $03, sawtooth: about 45 Hz. That is below the
                    bottom note of a piano - a buzz you feel rather than
                    hear as a note, which is why it reads as a beam
  explosion $889A   V3FREQHI $F0 down to $40: ~3.6 kHz falling to ~960 Hz,
                    repeated sfxRepeats times
  idle              V3FREQHI $04, about 60 Hz, left running between effects
  fanfare $8D16     all three voices at $40 - X, so $10 up to $3F:
                    ~240 Hz rising to ~950 Hz, ring-modulated sawtooth,
                    the sweep getting shorter each pass

These are derived from the constants in the code and the SID clock, not
measured. What would settle them exactly: a SID trace from an emulator.

args.text:
beryl signing off. Report written. Summary of what went into the project from my side:

GRAPHICS - no sprites at all; every object is a character from the games own 64-glyph font at $8E00, copied to $2000. One plot primitive ($8172, 35 callers) that reaches colour RAM by adding $D4 to the screen pointer high byte - verified with run_block. One read-back primitive ($818B, 9 callers) that is the entire collision system. Font mapped and stored as decoder dec_3g1jgm, so all five strings now read as English in the listing. Screen geometry, the palette and what each colour means at $0400 and $D800, including the ASCII mock-up of both screens. Four glyphs are dead art ($0B, $0C, $1C, $1F). $D016=$05 is 38-column mode and I could not tell whether it hides the lives digit - flagged rather than guessed.
